scenes.caption: Velocity is speed with a direction
scenes.narration: An athlete sprints 100 metres in 20 seconds: her speed is distance over time — 100 divided by 20, which is 5 metres per second. Velocity adds direction: she ran right, so her velocity is 5 metres per second rightwards.

shape.explain: The track: the straight path the athlete runs along.
The start mark: 0 metres.
The finish mark: 100 metres.
The athlete: she sprints 100 metres in 20 seconds.
The direction note: she ran to the right, which makes her 5 metres per second a velocity, not just a speed.
shape.text: direction: to the right  →  this is velocity

steps.text: Velocity is speed with a direction attached.

scenes.caption: Distance–time graphs: the gradient is the speed
scenes.narration: On a distance–time graph, time runs along the bottom and distance up the side: this line climbs 120 metres in 60 seconds. A probe travels the line while the gradient triangle builds beneath it — gradient is rise over run: 120 over 60, which is 2 metres per second.

shape.explain: The horizontal axis: time, from 0 to 60 seconds.
The vertical axis: distance, from 0 to 120 metres.
The time axis label: time runs from 0 to 60 seconds along the bottom.
The distance axis label: distance runs from 0 to 120 metres up the side.
The graph line: it climbs 120 metres in 60 seconds, a steady speed.
The run leg: the horizontal side of the gradient triangle, the time taken.
The rise leg: the vertical side of the gradient triangle, the distance covered.
The run value: 60 seconds of time.
The rise value: 120 metres of distance.
The reading rule: a steeper line means faster. A flat line means stopped.

steps.text: Distance–time gradient = speed. Rise over run.

scenes.caption: Velocity–time graphs: slope is acceleration, area is distance
scenes.narration: Now the vertical axis is velocity: the line rises from 0 to 20 metres per second in 10 seconds, so its slope is 20 over 10 — an acceleration of 2 metres per second squared. Watch the shaded area grow under the line as time passes: that area is the distance travelled — 100 metres.

shape.explain: The horizontal axis: time, from 0 to 10 seconds.
The vertical axis: velocity, from 0 to 20 metres per second.
The time axis label: time runs from 0 to 10 seconds along the bottom.
The velocity axis label: velocity runs from 0 to 20 metres per second up the side.
The graph line: velocity climbs from 0 to 20 metres per second in 10 seconds.
The acceleration working: the slope of the line gives 2 metres per second squared.
One of the shaded strips under the line: on a velocity-time graph, area is the distance travelled.
One of the shaded strips under the line: on a velocity-time graph, area is the distance travelled.
One of the shaded strips under the line: on a velocity-time graph, area is the distance travelled.
One of the shaded strips under the line: on a velocity-time graph, area is the distance travelled.
One of the shaded strips under the line: on a velocity-time graph, area is the distance travelled.
The distance working: half the rectangle gives the distance travelled.
The warning: the shaded shape is a triangle, not a rectangle, because the velocity is changing.

steps.text: Slope = acceleration. Area under the line = distance.

scenes.caption: Check the thinking
scenes.narration: Here is the classic trap: a runner jogs 400 metres down a track, turns, and jogs back in 100 seconds total. Distance is 800 metres, so speed is 8 metres per second — but displacement is zero, so velocity is zero.

shape.text: ❌ “Speed and velocity are the same thing.”

shape.explain: The track: the runner covers it twice, out and back.
The outward arrow: the first 400-metre leg of the run.
The outward label: 400 metres out.
The return arrow: the second 400-metre leg, back the way she came.
The return label: 400 metres back.
The runner: she finishes exactly where she started.
The corrected idea: velocity counts displacement. She ended where she began, so her velocity is zero.
shape.text: Velocity counts displacement — and she ended where she began.

steps.text: Speed uses distance. Velocity uses displacement.
